app.title: Map Projektor
compare.description: Compare the size of a country with another projection
compare.title: Compare
projection.aitoff.bestFor: Historical/reference use — mostly superseded today by its equal-area descendant, Hammer.
projection.aitoff.distorts: Both shape and area, moderately, worst near the outer edge of the ellipse.
projection.aitoff.name: Aitoff
projection.aitoff.preserves: Nothing exactly — neither conformal nor equal-area, a geometric compromise built for a pleasing outline.
projection.albers.bestFor: Mid-latitude regional maps of a single country or continent (its original purpose: the continental US).
projection.albers.distorts: Shape more and more the further a region sits from those two parallels — poor for global/equatorial use.
projection.albers.name: Albers
projection.albers.preserves: Area exactly, and shape stays accurate between its two standard parallels (here 20°N and 50°N).
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.bestFor: Maps centered on one point of interest where true area from that point matters (e.g. flight-range studies).
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.distorts: Shape more and more with distance from the center — regions near the antipode get squeezed into the outer rim.
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.name: Azimuthal Equal Area
projection.azimuthalEqualArea.preserves: Area exactly from its center point outward, and direction from that same center.
projection.eckert4.bestFor: Thematic climate/population maps — the same equal-area guarantee as Mollweide, gentler shape.
projection.eckert4.distorts: Shape at high latitudes, where landmasses compress toward the half-length pole lines.
projection.eckert4.name: Eckert IV
projection.eckert4.preserves: Area exactly, with a rounded outline that reads comfortably at world scale.
projection.equalEarth.bestFor: Modern replacement for Gall-Peters — true-size thematic maps that still look natural.
projection.equalEarth.distorts: Shape moderately near the poles, though far less severely than older equal-area projections.
projection.equalEarth.name: Equal Earth
projection.equalEarth.preserves: Area exactly, while keeping shapes visibly less stretched than Gall-Peters.
projection.equirectangular.bestFor: Simplicity and raw geographic data (it's just the coordinates), not display accuracy.
projection.equirectangular.distorts: Both shape and area, worsening toward the poles — a 1:1 lon/lat grid is not a neutral choice.
projection.equirectangular.name: Equirectangular
projection.equirectangular.preserves: Nothing exactly, but distances along meridians and the equator are true to scale.
projection.gallPeters.bestFor: Thematic maps where relative size matters more than recognizable shape (population, resources).
projection.gallPeters.distorts: Shape severely near the equator and poles — continents look visibly stretched vertically.
projection.gallPeters.name: Gall-Peters
projection.gallPeters.preserves: Area exactly — every landmass is shown at its true relative size.
projection.hammer.bestFor: Whole-sky/whole-world equal-area maps — astronomy's default for all-sky projections.
projection.hammer.distorts: Shape near the outer edge of the ellipse, though less severely than Aitoff or Mollweide.
projection.hammer.name: Hammer
projection.hammer.preserves: Area exactly, inheriting Aitoff's pleasing elliptical outline.
projection.mercator.bestFor: Nautical and aviation navigation, web maps at street-level zoom.
projection.mercator.distorts: Area, dramatically, away from the equator — Greenland appears larger than Africa despite being 14x smaller.
projection.mercator.name: Mercator
projection.mercator.preserves: Angles and shapes locally (conformal) — a straight line on the map is a constant compass bearing.
projection.mollweide.bestFor: Global thematic maps (e.g. star charts, world distributions) where area is what matters.
projection.mollweide.distorts: Shape strongly near the outer edge of the ellipse, especially at high latitudes.
projection.mollweide.name: Mollweide
projection.mollweide.preserves: Area exactly, within an elliptical world outline.
projection.naturalEarth.bestFor: Wall maps and general reference where visual appeal matters more than any measurable property.
projection.naturalEarth.distorts: Area and shape both, mildly, worst at high latitudes near the rounded poles.
projection.naturalEarth.name: Natural Earth
projection.naturalEarth.preserves: Nothing exactly — another eyeballed compromise, tuned specifically to look natural at a glance.
projection.orthographic.bestFor: Intuitive 'globe' views and showing a single hemisphere or region in spatial context.
projection.orthographic.distorts: Area and shape increasingly toward the visible edge (the limb), where the surface is nearly edge-on.
projection.orthographic.name: Orthographic
projection.orthographic.preserves: The visual perspective of a globe seen from space — the only projection here that looks like a sphere.
projection.polarNorth.bestFor: Polar-region maps and anything where 'distance from this one point' is the property that matters.
projection.polarNorth.distorts: Area and shape severely near the outer edge, where Antarctica is stretched into a ring around the map.
projection.polarNorth.name: North Polar
projection.polarNorth.preserves: Distance from the North Pole to anywhere else — that's the one property equidistant guarantees.
projection.polarSouth.bestFor: Southern-hemisphere and Antarctic-focused maps — a viewpoint almost never seen on a default world map.
projection.polarSouth.distorts: Area and shape severely near the outer edge, where the Arctic is stretched into the outer ring instead.
projection.polarSouth.name: South Polar
projection.polarSouth.preserves: Distance from the South Pole to anywhere else, same guarantee as the North Polar view mirrored.
projection.robinson.bestFor: General-purpose reference world maps where no single property needs to be exact.
projection.robinson.distorts: Everything a little (area, shape, distance) rather than any one thing a lot.
projection.robinson.name: Robinson
projection.robinson.preserves: Nothing exactly — it's a table-based compromise, tuned by eye rather than a strict formula.
projection.sinusoidal.bestFor: Historical interest and equal-area work that specifically needs true meridian distances.
projection.sinusoidal.distorts: Shape severely at the outer edges — a strong diagonal shear near high longitudes at high latitudes.
projection.sinusoidal.name: Sinusoidal
projection.sinusoidal.preserves: Area exactly, and distance is true along the equator and every meridian.
projection.winkelTripel.bestFor: General-purpose world reference maps — National Geographic's current standard for this reason.
projection.winkelTripel.distorts: A little of everything by design — the explicit tradeoff its name promises (a 'tripel' compromise).
projection.winkelTripel.name: Winkel Tripel
projection.winkelTripel.preserves: Nothing exactly, but keeps area, angle, and distance distortion all simultaneously low.
view.africa.description: Centred near 20°E, the middle of the African continent — the natural framing for atlases of Africa, and a reminder that Europe-centered is a choice, not a default of nature.
view.africa.name: Africa-centered
view.china.description: Common convention in Chinese school atlases — centred near 105°E, splitting the world along the Atlantic instead of the Pacific.
view.china.name: China-centered
view.southAmericaFlipped.description: South-up orientation, inspired by McArthur's Universal Corrective Map (1979) — a deliberate challenge to the assumption that "north = up".
view.southAmericaFlipped.name: South America (upside-down)
view.usaPacific.description: Common convention in American atlases — centred near 98°W, splitting the world through Europe and Africa.
view.usaPacific.name: USA / Pacific-centered
view.world.description: Default centering on the Greenwich meridian — the Atlantic-centred convention of most Western atlases, with Europe and West Africa in the middle.
view.world.name: Europe-centered
welcome.how1: Pick a projection on the left and the map morphs into it.
welcome.how2: Pick a view to recentre the map. Europe in the middle is a habit, not a law of nature.
welcome.how3: The buttons on the right of the map: a distortion grid (circles that show where a projection stretches things), light/dark mode, compare mode (see a country under a second projection) and i, for what the current projection preserves and distorts.
welcome.intro1: As we all know, the Earth is a sphere. (Sorry, flat earthers.)
welcome.intro2: Squashing it onto a flat map is where it gets awkward: shapes, areas, distances and directions can't all survive the trip, so every projection picks what to keep and what to bend. Each choice has its perks and its little lies. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.
welcome.intro3: This tool lets you see those trade-offs for yourself.
welcome.title: Welcome to Map Projektor!
